sample.note: 8 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 6 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This man’s Keystone Bridge Company built James Eads’s bridge across the Mississippi River at St. Louis, which opened in 1874. Years earlier, he had made his first big profits by investing in a company that built railroad sleeping cars.
tossups.r: He sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan in 1901. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born steel tycoon who later gave away most of his fortune.

tossups.p: An essay by this man opens by calling “the proper administration of wealth” the “problem of our age.” That essay argues that rich people should give away their fortunes during their own lifetimes to help the public.
tossups.r: That essay is _The Gospel of Wealth_. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon who paid for more than 2,500 public libraries.

tossups.p: As a teenager, this man became the secretary and telegraph operator of Thomas A. Scott at the Pennsylvania Railroad. When the Civil War began, he helped Scott organize the Union’s military railroads and telegraph lines.
tossups.r: He later made his fortune in Pittsburgh’s steel mills. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born industrialist who wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_.

tossups.p: This man was in Scotland in 1892 when his partner Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards to break a strike at one of his steel plants. The battle that followed left several workers and guards dead, and state troops took over the town.
tossups.r: That fight was the Homestead Strike. For 10 points, name this Pittsburgh steel tycoon and philanthropist.

tossups.p: Charles M. Schwab helped negotiate the 1901 sale of this man’s company for about 480 million dollars. The buyer combined that company with several others to create U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar corporation in history.
tossups.r: The buyer was J.P. Morgan. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born steel tycoon who spent his last years giving his money away.

tossups.p: This man offered 20 million dollars, the same amount the United States had paid Spain, so that the Philippines could buy its independence. He also founded the Church Peace Union and paid for the Peace Palace in The Hague.
tossups.r: He wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon and philanthropist.

tossups.p: After the 1889 Johnstown Flood, this member of the club that owned the failed South Fork Dam paid to give Johnstown a new library. Towns that accepted his library gifts had to provide the land and pay for the upkeep.
tossups.r: He funded more than 2,500 public libraries in all. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon and philanthropist.

tossups.p: A _Diplodocus_ skeleton nicknamed “Dippy” was dug up by an expedition from this man’s museum, and its species was named in his honor. He sent copies of that skeleton to museums in London, Paris, and other cities.
tossups.r: His partner Henry Clay Frick broke the 1892 Homestead Strike at one of his plants. For 10 points, name this Pittsburgh steel tycoon.

tossups.p: After rescuers died in a 1904 coal mine disaster near Pittsburgh, this man created a Hero Fund to honor people who risk their lives to save others. In 1910, he founded an Endowment for International Peace.
tossups.r: He believed rich people should give their money away while still alive. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon who funded thousands of libraries.

tossups.p: This man’s family left Dunfermline [“dun-FERM-lin”], Scotland, for Pennsylvania when he was 12, and his first job was as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill. Next he delivered messages for a telegraph office in Pittsburgh.
tossups.r: He later became one of the richest people in the world. For 10 points, name this steel tycoon who wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_.

tossups.p: This man named his first steel mill, the Edgar Thomson Works, after a railroad president he hoped would buy his rails. His company became a model of vertical integration, owning its own iron ore mines, coal fields, railroads, and ships.
tossups.r: His partner Henry Clay Frick first got rich selling coke, a fuel made from coal. For 10 points, name this Pittsburgh steel tycoon.

tossups.p: This man supported heavy taxes on large estates and wrote that “the man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.” He first published those ideas in an 1889 essay titled simply “Wealth” in the _North American Review_.
tossups.r: That essay became known as _The Gospel of Wealth_. For 10 points, name this philanthropist who made his fortune in steel.

tossups.p: In 1900, this man founded technical schools in Pittsburgh that later merged with an institute started by the family of banker Andrew Mellon. That school is now a university that bears both men’s names.
tossups.r: His partner Henry Clay Frick hired Pinkerton guards during the Homestead Strike. For 10 points, name this Scottish-born steel tycoon.

tossups.p: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky [“chy-KOFF-skee”] conducted at the opening festival of a New York concert hall, paid for by this man, that opened in 1891. This man also funded an institution for scientific research in Washington, D.C.
tossups.r: He made his fortune in steel and gave much of it away. For 10 points, name this philanthropist, the namesake of that famous concert hall.

tossups.p: This immigrant praised his adopted country’s progress in the 1886 book _Triumphant Democracy_. Critics called him a “robber baron,” while admirers saw this self-made man, who once worked in a cotton mill, as a “captain of industry.”
tossups.r: He sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan in 1901. For 10 points, name this Gilded Age tycoon who gave away most of his fortune.

clues.t: Scottish-born steel tycoon (1835–1919) who built his fortune in Pittsburgh
Philanthropist who gave away most of his fortune, funding more than 2,500 public libraries
Sold his steel company to J.P. Morgan in 1901 for about $480 million; Morgan made it the heart of U.S. Steel
His name is on a New York concert hall (opened 1891) and on a Pittsburgh university now shared with Andrew Mellon
Wrote _The Gospel of Wealth_ (1889): the rich should use their fortunes to help society
The Homestead Strike (1892) at his Pennsylvania steel plant ended in a deadly battle
His partner Henry Clay Frick ran the company and fought the union
Frick hired Pinkerton guards to break the Homestead Strike while the boss was away in Scotland
Left Dunfermline, Scotland, at 12 (1848); worked as a bobbin boy in a cotton mill, then as a telegraph messenger
Used vertical integration: his company owned its own iron ore mines, coal fields, railroads, and ships
Opened the Edgar Thomson Works (1875), using the Bessemer process to make cheap steel
Critics called him a “robber baron”; admirers called him a “captain of industry”
Founded the Keystone Bridge Company (1865), which built James Eads’s bridge at St. Louis (1874)
Mentor Thomas A. Scott hired him at the Pennsylvania Railroad; in the Civil War he helped run Union military railroads and telegraphs
_The Gospel of Wealth_ opens by calling “the proper administration of wealth” the “problem of our age”
“The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced”; he also backed heavy taxes on large estates
Charles M. Schwab negotiated the 1901 sale; U.S. Steel became the first billion-dollar corporation
Opposed taking over the Philippines and offered $20 million so it could buy its independence
Founded an Endowment for International Peace (1910) and the Church Peace Union; paid for the Peace Palace in The Hague
Paid for a new library in Johnstown after the 1889 Johnstown Flood; towns had to supply the land and upkeep for his libraries
“Dippy,” a _Diplodocus_ skeleton, belongs to a species named for him; he sent copies to museums around the world
Created a Hero Fund (1904) for people who risk their lives to save others
Wrote _Triumphant Democracy_ (1886), praising his adopted country
Funded a science institution in Washington, D.C.; Tchaikovsky conducted at his New York concert hall’s opening festival (1891)

trap.title: Which Carnegie built what?
trap.body: Lots of things carry the Carnegie name: Carnegie Hall, Carnegie Mellon University, and Dale Carnegie, the self-help author of _How to Win Friends and Influence People_, who was no relation. Players also mix up the Gilded Age tycoons: his partner Henry Clay Frick, oil king John D. Rockefeller, and banker J.P. Morgan. One real question even calls Carnegie the founder of U.S. Steel, but J.P. Morgan formed U.S. Steel in 1901 by buying Carnegie’s company.
trap.fix: Steel, Pittsburgh, Homestead, _The Gospel of Wealth_, and libraries mean Andrew Carnegie. Oil and Standard Oil mean Rockefeller; banking and creating U.S. Steel mean Morgan; the man who hired the Pinkertons is Frick.
trap.line: Real answer line: Andrew Carnegie (the same plain line in all 8 real tossups)

topics.name: California
topics.kicker: Pacific Coast state, admitted in 1850 · Missions, gold rush, and Hollywood
topics.briefing: California got its name from a make-believe island in a Spanish adventure story, and its real history is just as dramatic. Spanish priests built a chain of 21 missions along its coast, American settlers raised a grizzly-bear flag in 1846, and the discovery of gold at Sutter’s Mill in 1848 set off a rush that helped it become the 31st state in 1850.
topics.answerHtml: California (accept Alta California; prompt on Bear Flag Republic; do not accept “Baja California”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This state’s name comes from a fictional island ruled by Queen Calafia [“kuh-LAH-fee-uh”] in a Spanish adventure story written in the early 1500s by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo [“mon-TAHL-voh”]. For many years, European mapmakers wrongly drew this region as a giant island.
tossups.r: This state’s nickname is the Golden State, and its motto is “Eureka.” For 10 points, name this Pacific Coast state, home to Hollywood and Los Angeles.

tossups.p: In 1542, Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo [“kah-BREE-yoh”] sailed into San Diego Bay, becoming the first European to explore this region’s coast. Decades later, Francis Drake landed somewhere on this coast during his voyage around the world and claimed the land for England as “Nova Albion.”
tossups.r: In 1846, the Donner Party was trapped by snow in this state’s Sierra Nevada. For 10 points, name this Pacific Coast state whose capital is Sacramento.

tossups.p: Father Junípero Serra [“hoo-NEE-puh-roh SAIR-uh”] founded the first of this region’s 21 Spanish missions at San Diego in 1769, and the last one was built at Sonoma in 1823. Those missions were linked by a road called El Camino Real [“el kuh-MEE-noh ray-AHL”], or “the Royal Road.”
tossups.r: The cities of San Diego and San Francisco share their names with two of those missions. For 10 points, name this state where gold was found in 1848.

tossups.p: In 1812, the Russian-American Company built Fort Ross on this region’s northern coast, partly to hunt sea otters and to grow food for Russian settlements in Alaska. Russia sold that fort in 1841 to John Sutter, a settler from Switzerland whose own fort stood where this state’s capital later grew.
tossups.r: Gold was found at Sutter’s sawmill in 1848. For 10 points, name this state where the “forty-niners” rushed to find gold.

tossups.p: In June 1846, American settlers in Sonoma took the Mexican general Mariano Vallejo [“vuh-YAY-hoh”] prisoner and declared an independent republic. Their homemade flag showed a grizzly bear and a red star, and the explorer John C. Frémont [“FREE-mont”] soon took charge of their revolt.
tossups.r: A version of that bear flag became this state’s flag. For 10 points, name this state, which joined the Union in 1850.

tossups.p: Andrés Pico’s lancers clashed with soldiers under Stephen Kearny [“KAR-nee”] at the Battle of San Pasqual [“pahs-KWAHL”] in this region in late 1846. A few weeks later, Pico signed the Treaty of Cahuenga [“kuh-WENG-guh”] with John C. Frémont, ending the fighting here during the Mexican-American War.
tossups.r: In 1848, Mexico gave up this land in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. For 10 points, name this state where gold was discovered that same year.

tossups.p: On January 24, 1848, the carpenter James W. Marshall spotted shiny flakes in the water channel of a sawmill he was building at Coloma. Just nine days later, Mexico signed away this land in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, though neither side knew about Marshall’s find.
tossups.r: The next year, thousands of “forty-niners” rushed there. For 10 points, name this state where gold was found at Sutter’s Mill.

tossups.p: Delegates meeting at Monterey in 1849 wrote a constitution that banned slavery in this region, and they asked to join the Union without first becoming a territory. Henry Clay’s Compromise of 1850 admitted this state as a free state, upsetting the balance of free and slave states in the Senate.
tossups.r: It became the 31st state that year. For 10 points, name this state, which had grown quickly during a gold rush.

tossups.p: Charles Crocker hired thousands of Chinese workers to blast tunnels through the Sierra Nevada for a railroad company based in this state’s capital. Leland Stanford, one of that company’s “Big Four” leaders, took part in the golden spike ceremony at Promontory Summit in 1869 and later founded a university here.
tossups.r: That company was the Central Pacific. For 10 points, name this state at the western end of the first transcontinental railroad.

tossups.p: From 1910 to 1940, many Chinese immigrants were held for weeks or months at an immigration station on Angel Island, where some carved poems into the barrack walls. That island lies in a bay in this state, where the labor leader Denis Kearney had led an anti-Chinese movement with the slogan “The Chinese must go!”
tossups.r: Earlier, Chinese immigrants had called this land “Gold Mountain.” For 10 points, name this state whose largest city is Los Angeles.

tossups.p: After a 1906 disaster, the banker A. P. Giannini [“jah-NEE-nee”] carried his bank’s money to safety in a produce wagon and lent it out to help rebuild a city in this state; his Bank of Italy later became Bank of America. That disaster began with an April earthquake along the San Andreas Fault, followed by days of fires.
tossups.r: More than half of San Francisco’s people lost their homes. For 10 points, name this state, home to Los Angeles and Hollywood.

tossups.p: In 1864, Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant, which set aside a valley and a grove of giant sequoias in this state for public use. The Scottish-born naturalist John Muir later fought to protect that area and co-founded the Sierra Club in this state in 1892.
tossups.r: This state’s Sierra Nevada also includes Mount Whitney, the highest peak in the lower 48 states. For 10 points, name this state, which also contains Death Valley.

tossups.p: During World War II, the U.S. government forced more than 10,000 Japanese Americans to live at Manzanar, a camp in this state’s Owens Valley. Fred Korematsu, who was born in this state’s city of Oakland, challenged that forced removal in a famous Supreme Court case.
tossups.r: That removal followed Executive Order 9066 in 1942. For 10 points, name this West Coast state whose capital is Sacramento.

tossups.p: In 1965, Filipino American farmworkers led by Larry Itliong [“IT-lee-ong”] went on strike against grape growers near Delano [“duh-LAY-noh”] in this state, and Cesar Chavez’s union soon joined them. Chavez and Dolores Huerta [“WAIR-tuh”] then led a nationwide boycott of table grapes.
tossups.r: Their union became the United Farm Workers. For 10 points, name this state, home to the farm-rich Central Valley and the city of Los Angeles.

tossups.p: Earl Warren was elected this state’s governor three times before becoming Chief Justice of the United States in 1953. Ronald Reagan, a former actor, was governor of this state from 1967 to 1975, and Richard Nixon is the only U.S. president born in this state.
tossups.r: Both Reagan and Nixon have presidential libraries here. For 10 points, name this state, home to Hollywood.

clues.t: Nicknamed the Golden State; its motto is “Eureka” (“I have found it”)
Gold was found at Sutter’s Mill in 1848, and the “forty-niners” poured in during the gold rush of 1849
Capital: Sacramento; largest city: Los Angeles, home of Hollywood
Became the 31st state in 1850, as a free state under the Compromise of 1850
Father Junípero Serra founded the first of 21 Spanish missions (San Diego, 1769); El Camino Real linked them, and many Native people were forced to live and work there
Bear Flag Revolt (1846): settlers at Sonoma declared a republic under a grizzly-bear flag, which became the state flag
Won in the Mexican-American War; Mexico signed it away in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)
Central Pacific Railroad: built east from Sacramento by thousands of Chinese workers; its “Big Four” leaders included Leland Stanford
The 1906 San Francisco earthquake (San Andreas Fault) and fires left more than half the city homeless
Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant (1864); Scottish-born John Muir co-founded the Sierra Club (1892)
Has Mount Whitney, the highest peak in the lower 48 states, and Death Valley, the lowest point in North America
The Donner Party was trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada (1846–1847) while heading there
Chinese immigrants called it “Gold Mountain”
Named for a make-believe island ruled by Queen Calafia in a 1500s Spanish story by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo; old maps drew it as an island
Juan Rodríguez Cabrillo explored its coast (1542); Francis Drake claimed “Nova Albion” for England (1579)
Fort Ross (1812): a Russian outpost for hunting sea otters, sold to John Sutter in 1841
Bear Flaggers took Mexican general Mariano Vallejo prisoner; John C. Frémont soon took charge of the revolt
Andrés Pico fought Stephen Kearny at San Pasqual (1846), then signed the Treaty of Cahuenga with Frémont (1847)
James W. Marshall found gold at the sawmill in Coloma, nine days before the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
Its 1849 constitution, written at Monterey, banned slavery; it was never a U.S. territory
Charles Crocker’s Chinese crews blasted tunnels through the Sierra Nevada; Stanford joined the golden spike ceremony at Promontory Summit (1869)
Angel Island (1910–1940): Chinese immigrants were held there and carved poems into the walls; Denis Kearney’s slogan was “The Chinese must go!”
After the 1906 earthquake, A. P. Giannini lent money from his Bank of Italy (later Bank of America) to help San Francisco rebuild
Manzanar held more than 10,000 Japanese Americans after Executive Order 9066 (1942); Oakland-born Fred Korematsu challenged the removal
Delano grape strike (1965): Larry Itliong and Cesar Chavez; Dolores Huerta helped lead the grape boycott (United Farm Workers)
Earl Warren (governor, then Chief Justice) and Ronald Reagan (governor 1967–1975); Richard Nixon is the only president born there

trap.title: State or gold rush?
trap.body: Many clues for this state, like Sutter’s Mill, James Marshall, and the forty-niners, also lead tossups whose answer is the California gold rush, an event with its own answer line. If the question asks for “this event,” naming only the state is not enough. And Baja (Lower) California is a different place: a peninsula that belongs to Mexico.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this state” wants California, while “this event” or “this rush” wants “California gold rush.” The Spanish called the U.S. part Alta (Upper) California, so “Alta California” is fine, but never say “Baja.”
trap.line: Real answer line: California (accept Alta California; do not accept “Baja California”)

topics.name: New York
topics.kicker: The Empire State · From New Netherland to the Erie Canal
topics.briefing: New York began as New Netherland, a Dutch colony, until the English took over in 1664 and renamed it for the Duke of York. The Battles of Saratoga were fought there during the Revolution, and its biggest city became the nation’s first capital under the Constitution. When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, linking the Hudson River to the Great Lakes, that city grew into a booming port.
topics.answerHtml: New York (the state; accept New York State; do not accept “New York City”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Giovanni da Verrazzano [“vair-uh-ZAH-noh”] sailed into this region’s great harbor in 1524, and a bridge across the harbor’s entrance is named for him. In 1609, Henry Hudson sailed the _Half Moon_ up a river here while exploring for the Dutch East India Company.
tossups.r: That river is named for Hudson. For 10 points, name this state whose capital, Albany, sits on the Hudson River.

tossups.p: Peter Minuit [“MIN-yoo-it”] bought Manhattan Island from the Lenape [“leh-NAH-pay”] people in 1626 for trade goods worth 60 guilders. Decades later, the director-general Peter Stuyvesant [“STY-vuh-sunt”], who had a wooden leg, surrendered the Dutch colony here to an English fleet without a fight.
tossups.r: The English renamed the colony in 1664 for the Duke of York. For 10 points, name this state, whose largest city began as New Amsterdam.

tossups.p: According to tradition, the Peacemaker and Hiawatha [“hy-uh-WAH-thuh”] united the Mohawk, Oneida [“oh-NY-duh”], Onondaga [“on-un-DAW-guh”], Cayuga [“kay-YOO-guh”], and Seneca nations in this region under the Great Law of Peace, with the Onondaga keeping the central council fire. The Tuscarora [“tus-kuh-ROR-uh”] later joined them.
tossups.r: Those nations formed the Iroquois, or Haudenosaunee [“hoh-dee-noh-SHOH-nee”], Confederacy. For 10 points, name this state, whose largest city’s harbor holds Ellis Island and the Statue of Liberty.

tossups.p: Royal governor William Cosby had a printer arrested in this colony for newspaper articles attacking him. In 1735, the printer’s lawyer, Andrew Hamilton, argued that printing the truth could not be a crime, and a jury found the printer, John Peter Zenger, not guilty.
tossups.r: That case became a landmark for freedom of the press. For 10 points, name this colony, later the state whose capital is Albany.

tossups.p: Daniel Morgan’s riflemen fought at Freeman’s Farm and Bemis Heights in this state during a 1777 British campaign meant to cut New England off from the other colonies. At the end of that campaign, General John Burgoyne surrendered his whole army to Horatio Gates.
tossups.r: That victory at Saratoga helped convince France to join the war. For 10 points, name this state, whose capital, Albany, was Burgoyne’s goal.

tossups.p: In 1780, the American general commanding a fort on the Hudson River in this state secretly plotted to hand it over to the British. That plot was uncovered when Major John André [“AHN-dray”] was captured near Tarrytown with the fort’s plans hidden in his stockings.
tossups.r: The traitor, Benedict Arnold, escaped to the British. For 10 points, name this state, where West Point became home to the U.S. Military Academy in 1802.

tossups.p: At a 1788 convention in Poughkeepsie [“puh-KIP-see”], Alexander Hamilton led the fight for this state to ratify the Constitution over the objections of its longtime governor, George Clinton. _The Federalist Papers_ had first been printed in this state’s newspapers to win over its voters.
tossups.r: It became the 11th state to ratify. For 10 points, name this state, whose largest city was the first capital under the Constitution.

tossups.p: In 1807, Robert Fulton’s steamboat, later called the _Clermont_, carried passengers up a river in this state in about 32 hours of travel. In _Gibbons v. Ogden_, the Supreme Court later struck down a steamboat monopoly that this state had granted to Fulton and Robert Livingston.
tossups.r: Fulton’s boat steamed from Manhattan to Albany. For 10 points, name this state, whose largest city lies at the mouth of the Hudson River.

tossups.p: In 1825, Governor DeWitt Clinton held a “Wedding of the Waters” by pouring a keg of Lake Erie water into the Atlantic Ocean. Critics had mocked his project as “Clinton’s Ditch,” but it made shipping goods across this state far cheaper and faster.
tossups.r: That project, the Erie Canal, linked Buffalo to the Hudson River at Albany. For 10 points, name this “Empire State.”

tossups.p: Revivals led by preachers like Charles Grandison Finney swept this state’s western and central counties so often that the region was called the “burned-over district.” During that religious revival, Joseph Smith published the _Book of Mormon_ in the town of Palmyra here in 1830.
tossups.r: Rochester and Buffalo boomed along the Erie Canal in that region. For 10 points, name this state whose capital is Albany.

tossups.p: Susan B. Anthony was arrested for voting in Rochester in the 1872 presidential election and was fined 100 dollars, which she refused to pay. Earlier, Elizabeth Cady Stanton read her Declaration of Sentiments at a women’s rights convention in this state.
tossups.r: That 1848 convention met at Seneca Falls. For 10 points, name this state, where Stanton and Lucretia Mott organized the first women’s rights convention.

tossups.p: Frederick Douglass published his antislavery newspaper, _The North Star_, in Rochester in this state. In 1859, Senator William Seward sold Harriet Tubman a home in Auburn here, where she later opened a home for elderly African Americans in need.
tossups.r: Many freedom seekers on the Underground Railroad crossed this state to reach Canada near Niagara Falls. For 10 points, name this state, home to the Statue of Liberty.

tossups.p: Martin Van Buren, the first president born a citizen of the United States, grew up in this state’s village of Kinderhook and briefly served as its governor. Grover Cleveland, Theodore Roosevelt, and Franklin D. Roosevelt also governed this state before becoming president.
tossups.r: Franklin Roosevelt’s home at Hyde Park overlooks the Hudson River. For 10 points, name this state whose capital is Albany.

tossups.p: After the 1911 Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire killed 146 garment workers, this state created a commission whose work led to dozens of new workplace safety laws. Frances Perkins, who saw that fire, later became the first woman in a U.S. cabinet, under a former governor of this state.
tossups.r: That fire happened in Manhattan, near Washington Square. For 10 points, name this state, home to Long Island and the Adirondack Mountains.

tossups.p: Washington Irving gave this state’s largest city the nickname “Gotham,” set “Rip Van Winkle” in its Catskill Mountains, and set “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” near Tarrytown. Painters of the Hudson River School, led by Thomas Cole, also captured this state’s mountain scenery.
tossups.r: This state’s highest peak, Mount Marcy, rises in the Adirondack Mountains. For 10 points, name this state, which shares Niagara Falls with Canada.

clues.t: Capital: Albany, on the Hudson River; its largest city shares the state’s name
Nicknamed the Empire State; its motto is “Excelsior” (“ever upward”)
The Erie Canal (1825) linked the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo
Began as the Dutch colony of New Netherland; the English took over in 1664 and renamed it for the Duke of York
Ellis Island and the Statue of Liberty stand in its largest city’s harbor
Henry Hudson sailed the _Half Moon_ up its great river in 1609 for the Dutch East India Company
Peter Minuit bought Manhattan from the Lenape (1626); Peter Stuyvesant surrendered New Amsterdam to the English (1664)
Homeland of the Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) Confederacy: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and later Tuscarora
Battles of Saratoga (1777): John Burgoyne surrendered to Horatio Gates, and France joined the American side
Benedict Arnold plotted to hand West Point to the British (1780); it became the U.S. Military Academy (1802)
Its largest city was the first capital under the Constitution; it was the 11th state to ratify (1788)
Seneca Falls Convention (1848): Elizabeth Cady Stanton read the Declaration of Sentiments
Governors who became president: Martin Van Buren, Grover Cleveland, Theodore Roosevelt, and Franklin D. Roosevelt
Geography: the Adirondack Mountains (highest point, Mount Marcy), the Catskills, Long Island, and Niagara Falls
Giovanni da Verrazzano sailed into its harbor in 1524; the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge is named for him
The Peacemaker and Hiawatha united the nations under the Great Law of Peace; the Onondaga keep the council fire
Zenger trial (1735): Andrew Hamilton won freedom for printer John Peter Zenger, who had criticized Governor William Cosby
Major John André was captured near Tarrytown with West Point’s plans hidden in his stockings
Ratified at Poughkeepsie (1788) in a fight led by Alexander Hamilton, over Governor George Clinton’s objections; _The Federalist Papers_ first ran in its newspapers
Robert Fulton’s steamboat (the _Clermont_) went up the Hudson in 1807; _Gibbons v. Ogden_ struck down the state’s steamboat monopoly
DeWitt Clinton’s “Wedding of the Waters” (1825); critics had called the canal “Clinton’s Ditch”
The “burned-over district”: revivals by preachers like Charles Finney; Joseph Smith published the _Book of Mormon_ in Palmyra (1830)
Susan B. Anthony was arrested for voting in Rochester (1872) and refused to pay her $100 fine
Frederick Douglass printed _The North Star_ in Rochester; Harriet Tubman bought a home in Auburn from William Seward; freedom seekers crossed to Canada near Niagara Falls
Martin Van Buren of Kinderhook was the first president born a U.S. citizen
Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire (1911): 146 workers died, leading to new safety laws; Frances Perkins saw it
Washington Irving named its largest city “Gotham” and set “Rip Van Winkle” in the Catskills; Thomas Cole led the Hudson River School

trap.title: State or city?
trap.body: New York is the name of both a state and its biggest city, and real tossups treat them as separate answer lines. A city tossup (Broadway, Central Park, the five boroughs) wants the city, and answer lines for the city usually take plain “New York.” A state tossup (Albany, the Erie Canal, Saratoga, the Adirondacks) wants the state, so saying “New York City” there can be ruled wrong.
trap.fix: Listen for “this state” or “this colony” versus “this city.” For a state question, say just “New York” and stop. Upstate clues like Albany, Buffalo, Niagara Falls, and the Iroquois always mean the state.
trap.line: Real answer line: New York (the state; do not accept “New York City”)

topics.name: Boston Massacre
topics.kicker: Soldiers fire on a Boston crowd, March 1770 · A spark for the Revolution
topics.briefing: On a cold March night in 1770, with snow on the ground, an angry crowd in Boston threw snowballs, ice, and insults at British soldiers outside the Custom House. The soldiers fired into the crowd, and five colonists died, including Crispus Attucks. Paul Revere’s engraving of the scene spread outrage across the colonies, but John Adams defended the soldiers in court, and most of them were found not guilty.
topics.answerHtml: Boston Massacre (accept Incident on King Street; do not accept “Boston Tea Party”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Less than two weeks before this event, an 11-year-old boy named Christopher Seider [“SY-der”] was killed when a customs worker, Ebenezer Richardson, fired a gun from his house into a crowd of protesters. Samuel Adams helped organize a huge funeral for the boy, which raised anger against British officials in the same city.
tossups.r: In this event, British soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which five colonists died.

tossups.p: Three days before this event, a fight broke out at John Gray’s ropewalk, a rope-making yard, after a worker there insulted a soldier who was looking for a part-time job. Many off-duty British soldiers took such jobs for low pay, which angered local workers.
tossups.r: Days later, soldiers fired into a crowd on King Street. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which Crispus Attucks died.

tossups.p: This event began when a wigmaker’s apprentice named Edward Garrick insulted a British officer, and a sentry, Private Hugh White, struck the boy with his musket. A crowd soon surrounded White outside the Custom House, and Captain Thomas Preston marched seven soldiers to help him.
tossups.r: Those soldiers fired into the crowd on King Street. For 10 points, name this March 1770 event in which five colonists died.

tossups.p: On the same day as this event, Lord North asked Parliament to repeal most of the Townshend duties, keeping only the tax on tea. News crossed the Atlantic so slowly that colonists did not hear about that repeal until weeks after this event.
tossups.r: In this event, soldiers under Captain Thomas Preston fired on a crowd. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which Crispus Attucks was killed.

tossups.p: Henry Pelham accused a silversmith of copying his drawing of this event without permission. That silversmith’s hand-colored print of this event showed soldiers firing in a neat line on their captain’s order, an image that spread anger across the colonies.
tossups.r: That silversmith, Paul Revere, titled his print _The Bloody Massacre_. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which British soldiers killed five colonists.

tossups.p: Patrick Carr, who died more than a week after this event, told his doctor that he forgave the soldier who shot him and that he believed the soldiers had been provoked. That deathbed statement helped the defense at the trials that followed this event.
tossups.r: John Adams helped defend the British soldiers. For 10 points, name this 1770 event on King Street in which Crispus Attucks died.

tossups.p: The day after this event, a committee led by Samuel Adams demanded that acting governor Thomas Hutchinson remove British troops from the city. Hutchinson agreed to move both regiments to Castle William, a fort on an island in the harbor.
tossups.r: In this event, soldiers had fired into a crowd outside the Custom House. For 10 points, name this 1770 event that Paul Revere showed in a famous engraving.

tossups.p: After this event, a captain was tried separately from his men and found not guilty, because witnesses could not agree on whether he had ever given the order to fire. In a later trial, six of his soldiers were found not guilty and two were convicted of manslaughter.
tossups.r: That captain was Thomas Preston, and John Adams was the soldiers’ lawyer. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which British soldiers fired on a crowd in Boston.

tossups.p: Robert Treat Paine, a future signer of the Declaration of Independence, helped prosecute the eight soldiers accused in this event. Josiah Quincy Jr. joined their defense even though his own brother, Samuel Quincy, was one of the prosecutors.
tossups.r: Their most famous defense lawyer, John Adams, later became the second president. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which soldiers fired on a crowd on King Street.

tossups.p: Hugh Montgomery and Matthew Kilroy were the only soldiers convicted after this event, and both were found guilty of manslaughter rather than murder. They avoided a harsher punishment by claiming an old legal privilege called “benefit of clergy,” which could spare a first offender from the death penalty.
tossups.r: Their lawyer, John Adams, later became president. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which Crispus Attucks died.

tossups.p: During the trials that followed this event, a lawyer reminded the jury that “facts are stubborn things.” He argued that the soldiers had fired in self-defense after people in the crowd threw snowballs, ice, and clubs at them.
tossups.r: That lawyer, John Adams, defended the soldiers even though he supported the colonists’ cause. For 10 points, name this March 5, 1770, event in Boston.

tossups.p: From 1771 to 1783, Bostonians held a public speech every March 5 to remember this event, and Joseph Warren gave that speech in 1772 and again in 1775. John Hancock gave the 1774 speech, before July 4 took over as the town’s main patriotic holiday.
tossups.r: This event happened on King Street in 1770. For 10 points, name this clash in which British soldiers killed five colonists.

tossups.p: In 1858, abolitionists in Boston began holding a yearly celebration honoring the first person killed in this event, and in 1888 a monument to all of its victims was unveiled on Boston Common. That first victim was a sailor of African and Native American descent.
tossups.r: That victim was Crispus Attucks. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which British soldiers fired into a crowd.

tossups.p: A circle of cobblestones near the Old State House marks the spot of this event, on what was then called King Street. A lone sentry was guarding the Custom House, where customs money was kept, when an angry crowd gathered there.
tossups.r: Five colonists died there in March 1770. For 10 points, name this event that helped turn colonists against Britain.

tossups.p: The soldiers involved in this event belonged to the 29th Regiment, one of the units sent to the city in 1768 to protect customs officials collecting the Townshend duties. Colonists mocked those soldiers as “lobsterbacks” because of their red coats.
tossups.r: Paul Revere made a famous engraving of this event. For 10 points, name this 1770 event in which five colonists were killed on King Street.

clues.t: On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd of colonists in Boston
Five colonists died; Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native American descent, is remembered as the first to die
Paul Revere’s engraving of it spread anger across the colonies
John Adams defended the soldiers in court; most were found not guilty
Happened on King Street (later renamed State Street) outside the Custom House
Captain Thomas Preston led the soldiers; he was tried separately and found not guilty
The crowd threw snowballs, ice, and insults at the soldiers
British troops had been in the city since 1768 to protect customs officials collecting the Townshend duties
Of the eight soldiers tried, six were found not guilty and two were convicted of manslaughter
Samuel Adams used it to stir up anger and pressed to get the troops out of town
Less than two weeks earlier, customs worker Ebenezer Richardson killed 11-year-old Christopher Seider; Samuel Adams helped organize the funeral
A fight at John Gray’s ropewalk (March 2, 1770) started over soldiers taking part-time jobs
It began when apprentice Edward Garrick insulted an officer and the sentry, Private Hugh White, struck him
The same day, Lord North asked Parliament to repeal most Townshend duties, keeping the tax on tea
Revere copied Henry Pelham’s drawing; his print was titled _The Bloody Massacre_
Victim Patrick Carr told his doctor he forgave the soldier who shot him and thought the soldiers were provoked
Acting governor Thomas Hutchinson moved the troops to Castle William in the harbor
John Adams: “Facts are stubborn things”; he argued the soldiers fired in self-defense
Robert Treat Paine and Samuel Quincy prosecuted; Josiah Quincy Jr. helped John Adams defend the soldiers
Hugh Montgomery and Matthew Kilroy, convicted of manslaughter, escaped the death penalty by claiming “benefit of clergy”
Yearly March 5 speeches (1771–1783) by speakers such as Joseph Warren and John Hancock
Abolitionists began a yearly celebration honoring Crispus Attucks in 1858; a monument went up on Boston Common in 1888
A circle of cobblestones near the Old State House marks the spot
The soldiers were from the 29th Regiment; colonists mocked redcoats as “lobsterbacks”

trap.title: Massacre or Tea Party?
trap.body: Boston had two famous showdowns before the Revolution: the Boston Massacre (March 5, 1770), when soldiers fired into a crowd, and the Boston Tea Party (December 16, 1773), when the Sons of Liberty dumped tea into the harbor. Both involve Samuel Adams and British taxes, so buzzing early on “Boston” clues can go wrong. Some tossups instead want a person from this event: Crispus Attucks or John Adams.
trap.fix: Massacre clues: King Street, the Custom House, Captain Thomas Preston, snowballs, and Revere’s engraving. Tea Party clues: Griffin’s Wharf, the ship _Dartmouth_, disguises as Mohawk Indians, and the Tea Act. Listen for “this event” versus “this man” or “this lawyer.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Boston Massacre (accept Incident on King Street)

topics.name: Federalist Party
topics.kicker: One of the first two U.S. political parties · Party of Hamilton and John Adams
topics.briefing: George Washington warned against political parties, but his own cabinet split into the first two of them. The Federalists, led by Alexander Hamilton, wanted a strong national government, a national bank, and friendly ties with Britain, and John Adams became their only president. After New England Federalists protested the War of 1812 at the Hartford Convention, the party faded away.
accept: federalist party of the united states

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Rufus King, who had signed the Constitution for Massachusetts, became this party’s last presidential candidate in 1816, but he won only three states against James Monroe. After that loss, this party faded away during the so-called “Era of Good Feelings.”
tossups.r: This party’s only president was John Adams. For 10 points, name this party of Alexander Hamilton, the rival of the Democratic-Republicans.

tossups.p: Charles Cotesworth Pinckney was this party’s choice for vice president in 1800 and its candidate for president in 1804 and 1808, losing first to Thomas Jefferson and then to James Madison. Pinckney had earlier been one of the American diplomats asked for a bribe in the XYZ Affair.
tossups.r: This party’s leaders included John Adams and Alexander Hamilton. For 10 points, name this early political party that rivaled Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans.

tossups.p: John Fenno’s newspaper, the _Gazette of the United States_, supported this party, so Thomas Jefferson helped the poet Philip Freneau [“freh-NOH”] start the rival _National Gazette_ in 1791. Those newspapers spread the feud between this party and Jefferson’s supporters during George Washington’s presidency.
tossups.r: This party backed Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton’s plans. For 10 points, name this party that opposed the Democratic-Republicans.

tossups.p: Timothy Pickering, who was linked to a group of this party’s Massachusetts leaders called the Essex Junto [“JUN-toh”], plotted for New England to break away from the Union during Thomas Jefferson’s first term. Pickering hoped Aaron Burr would bring New York into that northern confederacy if Burr became its governor.
tossups.r: Burr lost that 1804 race and later killed this party’s leader, Alexander Hamilton, in a duel. For 10 points, name this party of John Adams.

tossups.p: George Cabot presided over a meeting of this party’s leaders where delegates proposed amendments such as requiring a two-thirds vote of Congress to declare war. Harrison Gray Otis and other messengers carried that meeting’s demands to Washington, arriving just as news of Andrew Jackson’s victory at New Orleans spread.
tossups.r: That meeting was the Hartford Convention, held during a war this party mocked as “Mr. Madison’s War.” For 10 points, name this party, which soon collapsed.

tossups.p: Weeks before losing power, this party’s Congress passed the Judiciary Act of 1801, which created sixteen new federal judgeships that its outgoing president filled with “midnight judges.” The next year, a Congress run by the rival party repealed that law.
tossups.r: That outgoing president, John Adams, also named John Marshall Chief Justice. For 10 points, name this party that lost power to Thomas Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans in 1801.

tossups.p: Members of this party in Congress passed a 1798 law under which Vermont congressman Matthew Lyon was jailed for criticizing President John Adams. Thomas Jefferson and James Madison secretly wrote resolutions for Kentucky and Virginia to protest that law and three others passed with it.
tossups.r: Those laws were the Alien and Sedition Acts. For 10 points, name this party that controlled Congress at the time, led by Alexander Hamilton and John Adams.

tossups.p: Fisher Ames of Massachusetts gave a famous speech in 1796 urging the House to pay for a treaty that this party supported and its rivals hated. That treaty, negotiated by John Jay, avoided war with Britain but did not stop the British from forcing American sailors into their navy.
tossups.r: Democratic-Republicans called this party too friendly to Britain. For 10 points, name this party that supported Jay’s Treaty and Alexander Hamilton.

tossups.p: The slogan “Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute” rallied this party after French agents demanded a bribe from American diplomats. That XYZ Affair helped this party gain seats in the 1798 elections and build up the navy for an undeclared war with France.
tossups.r: That war came under this party’s only president, John Adams. For 10 points, name this party of Alexander Hamilton.

tossups.p: In 1800, this party’s president fired Secretary of State Timothy Pickering and forced Secretary of War James McHenry to resign, because both men were more loyal to Alexander Hamilton. Hamilton then wrote a pamphlet attacking that president, which split this party before the election.
tossups.r: That president, John Adams, lost to Thomas Jefferson in 1800. For 10 points, name this party that never won the presidency again.

tossups.p: This party made a comeback in New England after Thomas Jefferson’s Embargo Act of 1807 hurt merchants and sailors there. Opponents of the embargo, many of them members of this party, mocked it with a cartoon snapping turtle named “Ograbme” [“oh-GRAB-mee”], which is “embargo” spelled backward.
tossups.r: This party had been led by Alexander Hamilton until his death in 1804. For 10 points, name this party of John Adams.

tossups.p: Many members of this party opposed the Louisiana Purchase, fearing that new western states would weaken the power of New England. This party drew much of its support from merchants, bankers, and lawyers in the Northeast who wanted close trade ties with Britain.
tossups.r: Its founder, Alexander Hamilton, created the First Bank of the United States. For 10 points, name this party, the opponent of Jefferson’s Democratic-Republicans.

tossups.p: This party supported a plan for the national government to take over the states’ war debts, and its leaders argued that the Constitution’s “necessary and proper” clause let Congress charter a bank. They favored a loose reading of the Constitution and a strong central government.
tossups.r: That plan came from Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton. For 10 points, name this political party that he led, the party of John Adams.

tossups.p: This party lost control of both the presidency and Congress in the election of 1800, which Thomas Jefferson later called a “revolution.” That handover was the first time power in the United States passed peacefully from one party to another.
tossups.r: This party’s candidate that year, John Adams, had been its only president. For 10 points, name this party built around Alexander Hamilton.

tossups.p: John Marshall, a Virginian from this party, served as Chief Justice for 34 years and kept its ideas about a strong national government alive long after the party itself died out. Marshall had been named Chief Justice in 1801 by this party’s only president.
tossups.r: That president was John Adams of Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this political party led by Alexander Hamilton.

clues.t: Led by Alexander Hamilton, the first Secretary of the Treasury
John Adams was its only president (1797–1801)
Rival of Thomas Jefferson and James Madison’s Democratic-Republican Party; together they were the first two U.S. parties
Wanted a strong national government, a national bank, and close ties with Britain
Its Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts (1798); Congressman Matthew Lyon was jailed under the Sedition Act
Hartford Convention (1814–1815): New England members protested the War of 1812, and the party collapsed
Supported Jay’s Treaty with Britain (1795), which its rivals hated
Lost the election of 1800, which Jefferson called a “revolution”: the first peaceful handover of power between parties
Strongest in New England, among merchants, bankers, and lawyers
Chief Justice John Marshall (1801–1835) kept its ideas alive on the Supreme Court for 34 years
Read the Constitution loosely: the “necessary and proper” clause let Congress create a national bank
Rufus King, its last presidential candidate (1816), won only three states against James Monroe; the party faded in the “Era of Good Feelings”
Charles Cotesworth Pinckney: vice-presidential pick in 1800, then lost the presidency to Jefferson (1804) and Madison (1808)
John Fenno’s _Gazette of the United States_ backed it; Jefferson helped Philip Freneau start the rival _National Gazette_ (1791)
Timothy Pickering, linked to the Essex Junto, plotted for New England to leave the Union and hoped Aaron Burr would join (1804)
George Cabot presided at Hartford; Harrison Gray Otis carried its demands, such as a two-thirds vote to declare war, to Washington
Judiciary Act of 1801: sixteen new judgeships filled with “midnight judges”; repealed in 1802
Jefferson and Madison’s Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions protested the Alien and Sedition Acts
Fisher Ames’s 1796 speech urged the House to fund Jay’s Treaty
XYZ Affair slogan: “Millions for defense, but not one cent for tribute”; the party gained seats in 1798
Adams fired Timothy Pickering and pushed out James McHenry (1800); Hamilton’s pamphlet attacking Adams split the party
Made a comeback in New England after Jefferson’s Embargo Act (1807), mocked by a cartoon snapping turtle named “Ograbme” (embargo spelled backward)
Many members opposed the Louisiana Purchase, fearing new western states would weaken New England
Members mocked the War of 1812 as “Mr. Madison’s War”

trap.title: Party, papers, or ratifiers?
trap.body: “Federalist” is part of three different answer lines. In 1787 and 1788, “Federalists” meant everyone who wanted to ratify the Constitution, including James Madison, against the Anti-Federalists. _The Federalist Papers_ were the 85 essays by Hamilton, Madison, and John Jay. The Federalist Party formed in the 1790s around Hamilton, and Madison helped lead the other side, the Democratic-Republicans.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun and the date. “This party” with clues from the 1790s to 1816 (Hamilton’s bank, John Adams, the Alien and Sedition Acts, the Hartford Convention) wants the Federalist Party; “these essays” wants _The Federalist Papers_. Never answer “Anti-Federalists” or “Democratic-Republicans” for Hamilton’s party.
